title: Getting Data Out
subtitle: SELECT — the command you will use more than every other command put together.

lessons.title: SELECT — asking the database a question
lessons.summary: SELECT *, choosing your own columns, and renaming them with AS.
lessons.examTip: SELECT column_list FROM table_name; The star means every column. AS renames a column in the output only — it does not change the table.

steps.title: SELECT star — show me everything
steps.expect: All six students, all six columns.

lines.text: Before we start, I have quietly put our six students back into the table, so we all have the same data in front of us.
Now, SELECT. This is the command you will type more than any other, for the rest of your working life.
SELECT means, show me. That is all it means.
Here it is, in its simplest form.
SELECT star FROM students.
The star is a wildcard. It means every column, do not leave anything out.
And FROM students tells it which table to look in.
So read the whole line in English. Show me everything from the students table.
Run.
There is our whole register.
Six students, six columns, all of it.
Now something important. Look at the table. Did SELECT change anything?
No. Nothing moved. SELECT only looks. It never touches your data.
That is why SELECT is the safe command. You can run it a thousand times and nothing can go wrong.

marks.cue: SELECT star FROM students
And FROM students tells it which table to look in

steps.title: Choosing only the columns you need
steps.sql:
SELECT first_name, surname, programme
FROM students;
steps.expect: Three columns only — no id, no date of birth, no fees.

lines.text: Now, the star is easy, but in real work it is often the wrong choice.
Think about it. If the principal asks for a list of names, does she want to see everybody's fees on that paper?
Certainly not. So we ask for only what we need.
So instead of the star, we write the names of the columns we want.
SELECT first_name, surname, programme, FROM students.
Notice the commas between the column names, and no comma before the word FROM.
Run.
Look at that. Much cleaner.
Three columns only. The fees are private, and they are not on the paper.
And here is a nice detail. The columns come out in the order you asked for them, not the order they sit in the table.
So you control the report. You are not stuck with the table design.

marks.cue: SELECT first_name, surname, programme, FROM students

steps.title: AS — giving a column a friendly name
steps.sql:
SELECT first_name AS Name,
       surname AS Surname,
       fees_paid AS AmountPaid
FROM students;
steps.expect: The same data, but the column headings now read Name, Surname and AmountPaid.

lines.text: One more thing before we start filtering, and this one makes your work look professional.
Our column names are fine for a programmer. first underscore name. fees underscore paid.
But you cannot hand that to the principal. It looks like computer talk.
So we rename them, just for the output. The keyword is AS.
Watch the headings as I type.
first_name AS Name. surname AS Surname. fees_paid AS AmountPaid.
Run.
Now look at the top of the result. Look at the headings.
Name. Surname. AmountPaid. Clean, readable, ready to print.
But listen carefully, because this is examinable.
AS only changes the heading in the answer. It does not rename the column in the table.
The table still says first_name. Nothing was altered. This is a nickname for one report, nothing more.
The proper word for that nickname is an alias. Write that word down. Alias.

marks.cue: first_name AS Name. surname AS Surname
fees_paid AS AmountPaid

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: SELECT questions carry the most marks on the whole paper, so let us get the habits right.
First. If the question says list all details, use the star. If it names the fields, list those fields. Read the question.
Second. The order is always SELECT, then FROM. What you want, then where it lives.
Third. Write it on two lines. SELECT and the columns on the first line, FROM and the table on the second.
It is easier to read, and when the query grows you will thank yourself.
And if they ask what an alias is: an alternative name given to a column or table in a query, to make the output more readable.
Now we know how to ask for columns. In the next lesson we learn how to ask for only certain rows.

items.cue: If the question says list all details
The order is always SELECT, then FROM
if they ask what an alias is
items.text: An alias is an alternative name given to a column or table in a query, to make the output more readable.

lessons.title: WHERE — filtering the rows
lessons.summary: Conditions, comparison operators, and joining conditions with AND, OR and NOT.
lessons.examTip: WHERE filters rows. Learn the operators: = equals, <> or != not equal, > greater than, < less than, >= and <=. Text in the condition must be in single quotes.

steps.title: Why we filter
steps.expect: Only the NC IT students — four of the six.

lines.text: Our table has six students. Imagine it had six thousand.
Nobody wants six thousand rows on their screen. They want the ones that matter.
So we add a filter. And the filter word is WHERE.
WHERE says, only give me the rows where this is true.
Watch the third line.
WHERE programme equals, in single quotes, NC IT.
Notice the quotes again. NC IT is text, so it must be in single quotes.
And notice we use one equals sign, not two. In SQL, one equals sign asks the question.
If you have done programming, you must unlearn the double equals here. SQL uses one.
Run.
Look at that.
Four students, and every one of them is doing NC IT.
Farai in Accounting is not there. Blessing in Marketing is not there.
The rows did not disappear from the table. They are still safe. WHERE only decided who to show us.

marks.cue: WHERE programme equals, in single quotes, NC IT
And notice we use one equals sign

steps.title: The comparison operators
steps.expect: Only students who have paid more than one hundred dollars.

lines.text: Equals is only one of the operators. Let me give you the whole set, because the exam uses all of them.
The equals sign, for is exactly this.
Greater than, and less than. You know those signs from mathematics.
Greater than or equal to, which is the greater than sign followed by an equals sign.
Less than or equal to, the same way.
And not equal to, which is written as less than followed by greater than. Some systems also accept an exclamation mark and an equals sign.
Now, the money question. Which students have paid more than one hundred dollars?
So here we write WHERE fees_paid greater than one hundred.
And this time, no quotes. One hundred is a number, and we are comparing it as a number.
If you put quotes around a number, the database compares it as text, and text compares letter by letter. Your answer comes out wrong.
Run.
There we are.
Tanaka, Rudo, Chipo and Kuda have all paid over one hundred.
Farai, who has paid nothing, and Blessing, who has paid seventy five, are not on the list.

marks.cue: So here we write WHERE fees_paid greater than one hundred

steps.title: AND, OR and NOT
steps.sql:
SELECT first_name, surname, programme, fees_paid
FROM students
WHERE programme = 'NC IT'
  AND fees_paid > 200;
steps.expect: Only NC IT students who have also paid more than two hundred.

lines.text: Now the real world. Real questions have more than one condition.
The bursar says, give me the NC IT students who have paid more than two hundred dollars.
That is two conditions in one question, and both must be true.
When both must be true, we join them with AND.
Look at the condition.
WHERE programme equals NC IT, AND fees_paid greater than two hundred.
See how I put AND on its own line, lined up underneath? Do that. It makes long queries readable.
Run.
Three students survived that filter.
Rudo, Chipo and Kuda. All three are in NC IT, and all three have paid more than two hundred.
Now look carefully at Rudo. She has paid two hundred point five zero.
That is more than two hundred, by fifty cents, so she is in. Always check the boundary cases like that one.
If the question had said two hundred or more, we would have used greater than or equal to instead.
Now the other two joiners. OR means only one of them needs to be true.
And NOT reverses a condition. WHERE NOT programme equals NC IT gives you everybody who is not in IT.
AND is strict. OR is generous. NOT turns it around. That is all three.

marks.cue: WHERE programme equals NC IT, AND fees_paid greater than two hundred

steps.title: OR, and why brackets matter
steps.sql:
SELECT first_name, surname, programme, fees_paid
FROM students
WHERE (programme = 'NC Accounting' OR programme = 'NC Marketing')
  AND fees_paid < 100;
steps.expect: Accounting or Marketing students who owe money — Farai and Blessing.

lines.text: Now I want to show you the trap that catches even good students.
The question is: give me the Accounting or Marketing students who have paid less than one hundred.
Look at the brackets I am putting in.
Open bracket, programme equals NC Accounting OR programme equals NC Marketing, close bracket.
And then AND fees_paid less than one hundred.
Why the brackets? Because AND is stronger than OR. The database does AND first, just like multiplication before addition.
Without the brackets, the computer would read it as: all Accounting students, OR Marketing students who owe money.
That is a completely different question, and you would lose the mark.
So when you mix AND and OR in one WHERE, put brackets around the OR part. Every time.
Run.
Farai and Blessing.
Farai is Accounting and has paid nothing. Blessing is Marketing and has paid seventy five.
Exactly the two people the bursar needs to phone this afternoon.

marks.cue: Open bracket, programme equals NC Accounting OR programme equals NC Marketing, close bracket
And then AND fees_paid less than one hundred

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: WHERE questions are where most of the practical marks live, so listen to this part twice.
The question will be in English. Something like, list the names of students in NC IT who have paid more than two hundred dollars.
Here is how you translate it, every time, in the same order.
One. What do they want to see? Names. That is your SELECT line.
Two. Where does it live? The students table. That is your FROM line.
Three. Which rows? IT students who paid over two hundred. That is your WHERE line.
Read the English, underline the nouns for SELECT, and underline the conditions for WHERE.
Then check the quotes. Text yes, numbers no.
And if the word or appears in the question together with the word and, reach for your brackets immediately.

items.cue: The question will be in English
items.text: "List the names of students in NC IT who have paid more than two hundred dollars."

items.cue: One. What do they want to see

steps.label: What do they want to see?

items.text: Underline the nouns → SELECT.   Underline the conditions → WHERE.
AND together with OR?  Bracket the OR part:  WHERE (a OR b) AND c

lessons.title: LIKE, IN, BETWEEN and IS NULL
lessons.summary: Searching for patterns, lists of values, ranges, and missing data.
lessons.examTip: LIKE with % matches any number of characters, and _ matches exactly one. IN checks a list. BETWEEN checks a range and includes both ends. IS NULL finds missing data — never write = NULL.

steps.title: LIKE and the percent wildcard
steps.expect: Every student whose surname starts with M.

lines.text: Sometimes you do not know the whole value. You only know part of it.
The office says, find me all the students whose surname starts with M.
You cannot use equals for that, because equals means exactly this and nothing else.
So we use LIKE, and we use a wildcard.
So we write LIKE, and then the pattern in quotes.
M, followed by the percent sign.
The percent sign means, any number of characters, and I do not care what they are.
So M percent means, starts with M, then anything.
Run.
Moyo, Mpofu.
Both surnames start with M, and the rest of the letters did not matter.
Now learn the three patterns, because the exam will ask for all three.
M percent means starts with M.
Percent M means ends with M.
Percent M percent means contains M anywhere inside.
Front, back, both sides. Where you put the percent sign is the whole answer.

marks.cue: So we write LIKE, and then the pattern in quotes
M, followed by the percent sign

steps.title: The underscore wildcard
steps.expect: Dube — four letters, ending in u-b-e.

lines.text: There is a second wildcard, and it is the one students forget.
The underscore. And it means exactly one character. Not more, not less. Exactly one.
Look at this pattern.
Underscore, u, b, e.
Read it as: one character I do not know, then u, then b, then e.
So it will match a four letter surname ending in u b e.
Run.
Dube.
D is the unknown character, and then u b e.
Ncube did not match. Why not? Count the letters.
N c u b e is five letters. Our pattern only allowed four. One underscore, one character.
So remember the difference, and say it out loud. Percent is any amount. Underscore is exactly one.

marks.cue: Underscore, u, b, e

steps.title: IN and BETWEEN
steps.expect: The second query wins the screen — students who paid between 100 and 400 inclusive.

lines.text: Two shortcuts now, and both of them make your queries shorter and easier to read.
The first one uses IN.
Remember in the last lesson we wrote programme equals Accounting OR programme equals Marketing?
That gets very long when there are five programmes. So IN gives you a list instead.
WHERE programme IN, then the list in brackets, separated by commas.
It means, is this value one of these? IN is just a tidy OR.
The second one uses BETWEEN, for ranges.
WHERE fees_paid BETWEEN one hundred AND four hundred.
And here is the detail the exam checks. BETWEEN includes both ends.
Exactly one hundred is included. Exactly four hundred is included. It is not just the numbers in the middle.
Run.
The console shows us the last query, so we are looking at the BETWEEN result.
Tanaka, Rudo and Chipo. One fifty, two hundred point five, and three twenty. All inside the range.
Kuda paid one thousand two hundred, so he is above the range and he is out.

marks.cue: WHERE programme IN, then the list in brackets
WHERE fees_paid BETWEEN one hundred AND four hundred

steps.title: IS NULL — finding what is missing
steps.expect: Memory Mpofu — the one student whose date of birth was never captured.

lines.text: Now the last one, and this is the one that catches everybody, so pay attention.
Sometimes you need to find the records where something is missing.
The registrar says, which students have no date of birth captured? We must phone them.
Now your instinct will be to write WHERE date_of_birth equals NULL. Do not do it. It will never work.
Here is why. NULL does not mean a value. NULL means unknown.
And you cannot ask whether one unknown thing equals another unknown thing. The database cannot answer that.
So we write IS NULL instead.
WHERE date_of_birth IS NULL. Two words, no equals sign anywhere.
Run.
Memory Mpofu.
Her record went in without a date of birth, and now we have found her.
And the opposite is IS NOT NULL, for records where the field was filled in.
Write this on your hand if you must. Never equals NULL. Always IS NULL.

marks.cue: WHERE date_of_birth IS NULL. Two words

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: Four tools in this lesson, and the exam has a favourite way of asking for each one.
When the question says starting with, ending with, or containing, they want LIKE and a percent sign.
When the question lists two or three specific values, IN is the neat answer, but a chain of ORs also gets full marks.
When the question says between two numbers or between two dates, use BETWEEN, and remember both ends are included.
And when the question says has not been entered, is missing, or is blank, that is IS NULL.
One more marker's favourite. State the difference between the percent sign and the underscore in a LIKE clause.
Answer. The percent sign represents any number of characters, including none. The underscore represents exactly one character.
Learn that sentence. It is one mark, and it is free.

items.cue: When the question says starting with
When the question lists two or three specific values
State the difference between the percent sign and the underscore

lessons.title: ORDER BY, DISTINCT and LIMIT
lessons.summary: Sorting your answer, removing repeats, and asking for only the top few rows.
lessons.examTip: ORDER BY sorts — ASC is smallest first and is the default, DESC is largest first. DISTINCT removes duplicate values. LIMIT restricts how many rows come back.

steps.title: ORDER BY — putting it in order
steps.expect: The same students, now in alphabetical order by surname.

lines.text: Look at the answers we have been getting. They come out in whatever order the database feels like.
That is fine for us, but it is not fine for a class list on the notice board.
A class list must be alphabetical. So we sort it.
So we add ORDER BY at the bottom of the query.
ORDER BY surname ASC.
A S C is short for ascending, which means going up. A to Z for text, smallest to largest for numbers.
Run.
Now look at that. A proper class list.
Banda, Dube, Moyo, Ncube, Sibanda, Zhou. Straight down the alphabet.
And a small point that saves you writing. ASC is the default.
If you write ORDER BY surname and say nothing else, you still get ascending. But write it anyway, so the marker can see you know it.

marks.cue: ORDER BY surname ASC

steps.title: DESC — biggest first
steps.expect: The biggest payer at the top, the smallest at the bottom.

lines.text: Now turn it upside down.
The bursar does not want alphabetical. She wants to see who has paid the most, at the top.
So DESC, short for descending, which means going down.
ORDER BY fees_paid DESC. Largest amount first.
Run.
Kuda at the top, with one thousand two hundred and fifty.
And right at the bottom, Farai, with zero. He has paid nothing.
See how much that one word tells you? The whole story of the fees, in one glance.
And you can sort by more than one column. ORDER BY programme ASC, comma, surname ASC.
That groups them by programme, and inside each programme it puts them in alphabetical order. Very useful for real reports.

marks.cue: ORDER BY fees_paid DESC. Largest amount first

steps.title: DISTINCT — one of each
steps.expect: Three rows — each programme listed once, no repeats.

lines.text: Here is a real question from the registry. What programmes do we actually run?
Now if I just say SELECT programme FROM students, what do I get?
I get NC IT four times, because four students are doing it. That is a mess.
I want each programme listed once. So we add DISTINCT.
SELECT DISTINCT programme FROM students.
DISTINCT goes right after SELECT, before the column name. Not at the end.
Run.
Three rows.
NC IT, NC Accounting, NC Marketing. Each one exactly once.
That is our programme list, and we got it out of the student data without keeping a separate list anywhere.

marks.cue: SELECT DISTINCT programme FROM students

steps.title: LIMIT — just the top few
steps.sql:
SELECT first_name, surname, fees_paid
FROM students
ORDER BY fees_paid DESC
LIMIT 3;
steps.expect: Exactly three rows — the three biggest payers.

lines.text: Last one for this chapter, and it is the one that makes top ten lists.
The principal says, show me the three students who have paid the most.
Notice you need two things there. You need the order, and you need to cut it off after three.
So look at the last line.
First ORDER BY fees_paid DESC, so the biggest is at the top.
Then LIMIT three, which says stop after three rows.
And the order matters. LIMIT must come last, after ORDER BY. Always at the very bottom.
Because if you cut first and sort afterwards, you get three random students in a neat order. Wrong answer.
Run.
Exactly three.
Kuda, Chipo, Rudo. The three biggest payers in the college.
One note for the exam. LIMIT is the MySQL word, and MySQL is what we use, so LIMIT is correct for you.
But in Microsoft SQL Server the same job is done by SELECT TOP three. If a question mentions SQL Server, use TOP.

marks.cue: First ORDER BY fees_paid DESC
Then LIMIT three, which says stop after three rows

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: Let us put the whole SELECT together now, because the order of the clauses is a mark on its own.
SELECT, then FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT.
Say it again with me. SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
We have not done GROUP BY and HAVING yet. They are waiting for you in Chapter Seven.
But the order never changes, in any query, in any exam, anywhere in the world.
If you write ORDER BY before WHERE, the query fails, and it fails for a reason the marker can see instantly.
So when a question is long and you feel panic coming, write the seven words down the side of your page first.
Then fill in the ones you need and cross out the ones you do not. You will never write them in the wrong order again.

items.cue: the order of the clauses is a mark on its own
